equation_request.abstract: Noise is often regarded as anathema to quantum computation, but in some settings it can be an unlikely ally. We consider the problem of learning the class of $n$-bit parity functions by making queries to a quantum example oracle. In the absence of noise, quantum and classical parity learning are easy and almost equally powerful, both information-theoretically and computationally. We show that in the presence of noise this story changes dramatically. Indeed, the classical learning problem is believed to be intractable, while the quantum version remains efficient. Depolarizing the qubits at the oracle’s output at any constant nonzero rate does not increase the computational (or query) complexity of quantum learning more than logarithmically. However, the problem of learning from corresponding classical examples is the Learning Parity with Noise (LPN) problem, for which the best known algorithms have superpolynomial complexity. This creates the possibility of observing a quantum advantage with a few hundred noisy qubits. The presence of noise is essential for creating this quantum-classical separation.

specification.problem: Learn a hidden n-bit parity function f_s(x)=s·x mod 2 from a quantum example oracle whose output qubits are depolarized at constant rate, versus classical noisy examples (LPN).
specification.reconstruction_scope: Smallest useful construction: standard noiseless quantum parity learning via a quantum example state and Hadamard transform, plus a depolarizing channel on the output qubits, for a tiny assumed instance n=3, s=101. The paper's specific noisy-learning algorithm, its complexity bounds, and the LPN hardness/separation arguments are outside this scope.

equations.label: Parity function
equations.description: Target concept class of n-bit parities.
equations.abstract_quote: learning the class of $n$-bit parity functions
equations.justification: Parity functions are defined by a hidden string s; the explicit form is standard.
assumptions: Parity is s·x mod 2 with no affine offset

equations.label: Quantum example state
equations.description: Assumed form of a uniform-superposition quantum example.
equations.justification: Standard quantum PAC example oracle for the uniform distribution; the abstract names a quantum example oracle without defining it.

equations.label: Noiseless Fourier sampling
equations.latex: H^{\otimes n}\otimes H\,|\psi_s\rangle \;\Rightarrow\; \text{measuring the first } n \text{ qubits gives } s \text{ with probability } 1
equations.description: Hadamard transform on the n input qubits and the label qubit; the label-qubit measurement yields 1 with probability 1/2, and conditioning on 1 leaves the input register in |s>. Equivalent to Bernstein-Vazirani-style learning.
equations.justification: Background for noiseless quantum parity learning; the abstract says only that noiseless learning is easy.
assumptions: Post-select on the label qubit being 1, or equivalently use the phase-state form

equations.label: Depolarizing channel
equations.description: Depolarizing noise applied to each oracle output qubit.
equations.justification: The abstract states depolarizing at a constant nonzero rate; this parametrization is assumed.
assumptions: Independent single-qubit channel on each output qubit

equations.label: Classical noisy examples (LPN)
equations.latex: (a,b)\text{ with } a\sim U(\{0,1\}^n),\; b=s\cdot a\oplus e,\; e\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\epsilon)
equations.description: Classical examples with label noise, the LPN problem.
equations.abstract_quote: the problem of learning from corresponding classical examples is the Learning Parity with Noise (LPN) problem
equations.justification: Standard LPN definition; the noise rate epsilon is not given in the abstract.

specification.initial_state: Quantum example state |psi_s> (assumed uniform superposition) prepared by the oracle, then optionally depolarized.

steps.description: Query the quantum example oracle to obtain |psi_s> for the assumed instance n=3, s=101.
Optionally apply depolarizing noise to the output qubits.
Apply Hadamards to all qubits and measure; in the noiseless case this reveals s.

specification.measurement: Computational-basis measurement of all qubits after Hadamards (noiseless baseline only).
specification.classical_postprocessing: Noiseless: read s directly from X when B=1. Noisy case: the paper's postprocessing is not specified in the abstract, so it is omitted here.
assumptions: Tiny instance n=3, s=101 chosen for illustration
